title: What do I have for this?
hookLine: for each event, ask which power you have to meet it: patience for insult, endurance for hard work (Enchiridion 10)
carry: feel its weight in your hand

lines: WHAT DO I HAVE FOR THIS?
cards: A plumber shows up at a flooded basement. She doesn't stand in the doorway saying, why me, why water, why today. She opens her bag.
Wrench, tape, a pump. The question in her head is practical: what do I have for this? Most of us meet trouble the other way round.
We describe it, complain about it, replay it. Epictetus suggests carrying a bag like the plumber's, only the tools are inside you.

teach.b: With everything that happens to you, Epictetus says in section ten of the handbook, turn toward yourself and ask what power you have for dealing with it.

The word for power is dynamis, the root English borrowed for dynamic and dynamite. He gives three examples. If you see someone very beautiful and feel the pull, you'll find you have self-control for that.
If hard work lands on you, endurance.
If someone insults you, patience. Three troubles, three tools, each already in the bag.

Notice what he's assuming: that for every kind of event, there's some human strength that fits it. Not that you'll enjoy it. That you're equipped for it, at least a little, and the equipment gets stronger with use.
Elsewhere, in the Discourses, he says it more sharply: difficulties are what show who people are. Then the habit. If you get used to asking the question, he says, the impressions won't carry you off.
Without the question, a hard day picks you up and runs.
With it, there's a pause, a hand reaching into the bag, and a choice of tool. Maybe patience is thin today, or endurance is low. Fine.
Asking still turns you from someone things happen to into someone deciding how to meet them.

teach.h: WHAT DO I HAVE FOR THIS?
teach.b: And the list is longer than three. Courage for a hard phone call. Gentleness for a child melting down.
Humor for a ruined dinner. Honesty for a mistake at work.

how: Some Stoic practitioners meet a difficulty by asking which strength it calls for, such as patience, endurance or courage, before reacting.

o: explosive energy that blasts a problem away
a burst of motivation that comes from outside
power: the strength you find to meet each event

games.q: what do I have for this — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus gives three examples of troubles and the strength for each
self-control for beauty, endurance for labor, patience for insult.
section ten says to ask why this is happening to you
it says to ask what power you have to deal with it.
the habit, he says, keeps impressions from carrying you off
asking the question puts a pause between the event and you.

games.q: someone insults you in front of colleagues. which tool does Epictetus say you'll find in the bag?
games.why: for insult, he says, you'll find patience; for hard work, endurance; for a strong attraction, self-control.

practice: Bring to mind one trouble you're carrying this week, a deadline, a difficult person, a worry, an ache, and ask Epictetus' question slowly: what do I have for this? Wait for a word to come: patience, courage, humor, honesty, rest.
Picture taking that one tool out of the bag, and feel its weight in your hand.

wordCard.voice: Dynamis, the power or strength Epictetus asks us to find for every event: self-control, endurance, patience, or another. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 10: power, ability; the root of dynamic and dynamite.

carryVoice: Your line: feel its weight in your hand. Every trouble comes with some strength that fits it. Day three hundred forty-two, done.
